clinicalPearls: Recurrent sensation of abdominal bloating or visible distension not sufficiently explained by another disorder
Bloating is the subjective feeling of pressure, whereas distension is a measurable increase in abdominal girth, and they may occur together or separately
Symptoms typically worsen through the day and after meals and improve overnight
It frequently overlaps with other functional gut disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome and constipation
Organic causes such as carbohydrate malabsorption, bacterial overgrowth and, importantly, ovarian and other intra-abdominal pathology should be considered
Management addresses coexisting constipation, dietary triggers and, in some, gut microbiota and abdominal wall behaviour
reference.pathophysiology: Functional abdominal bloating and distension arise from a combination of factors including altered handling and perception of intestinal gas, visceral hypersensitivity, abnormal abdominal wall muscle behaviour (an abdomino-phrenic dyssynergia in which the diaphragm descends and the abdominal wall relaxes), and changes in gut microbiota and fermentation. These mechanisms produce the sensation of bloating and, when the abdominal wall protrudes, visible distension, without a defining structural abnormality. Overlap with other functional gut disorders reflects shared gut-brain mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Irritable bowel syndrome and functional constipation
Ovarian or other intra-abdominal mass or ascites
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of the pattern and diurnal variation of symptoms
Coeliac serology and assessment for carbohydrate malabsorption where indicated
Consideration of breath testing for bacterial overgrowth
Imaging or gynaecological assessment if an organic mass or ascites is suspected
Review of coexisting constipation as a driver
redFlags: Persistent distension with weight loss or a palpable mass
New symptoms in an older woman raising concern for ovarian pathology
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and often chronic, with symptoms fluctuating; many patients improve when coexisting constipation and dietary triggers are addressed.
pitfalls: Overlooking ovarian or other intra-abdominal pathology causing distension
Attributing all bloating to gas rather than abdominal wall behaviour
Missing carbohydrate malabsorption or bacterial overgrowth
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Treat coexisting constipation with laxatives, as it is a key reversible driver of bloating and distension
Dietary modification, including a trial of a low-FODMAP diet and reduction of fermentable, gas-producing foods
Probiotics or a trial of the non-absorbable antibiotic rifaximin where bacterial overgrowth is suspected
Antispasmodics or peppermint oil for associated abdominal discomfort
Neuromodulators such as low-dose tricyclic antidepressants for visceral hypersensitivity in refractory cases
Biofeedback and diaphragmatic-abdominal retraining for abdomino-phrenic dyssynergia
Exclude organic disease, including ovarian and other intra-abdominal pathology, before settling on the diagnosis
